source: Bramley, Jones, Gureckis, Ruggeri (2022) Children's failure to control variables may reflect adaptive decision-making
finding: Switch-box task: find the one working (sparse) or broken (dense) switch among six. Children were told which. Testing several switches at once is the best play when only one cause exists. Testing one at a time (CVS) is the only good play when all but one work. Children shifted their strategy with the sparsity cue.
numbers: N=104 children (53 aged 7-9, 51 aged 10-13). Six tokens, one per test. Expected return: about 1.90 with split-half in sparse, 1.25 with one-at-a-time in dense. Power analysis: about 25 per cell for 80% power.
quote: children can perform and interpret controlled experiments, are sensitive to causal sparsity, and use this information to tailor their testing strategies
limits: Binary, disjunctive switches, not the classic ramps or springs. CVS is done by leaving variables off, not by holding them fixed. Museum sample; 12 children dropped from later analyses for technical faults.
agent_relevance: CVS is not always the best test. When few causes are expected, grouped tests win. S4 'one change per test' should be the default for dense or unknown causal structure, with a sparse-cause exception.

source: Bramley, Jones, Gureckis, Ruggeri (2022) Children's failure to control variables may reflect adaptive decision-making (first-test results)
finding: On the very first test, older children more often switched on several switches, and the sparse condition pulled both age groups toward testing several. No age by condition interaction, so both ages were similarly sensitive to sparsity.
numbers: First test, test-one share: 7-9 sparse 15/24 (62.5%), 7-9 dense 23/29 (79.3%), 10-13 sparse 11/28 (39.3%), 10-13 dense 14/23 (60.9%). Age OR 2.24 (95% CI 1.05-4.9, BF 3.44). Condition OR 0.47 (CI 0.22-1.01, BF 2.34). Interaction BF 0.57. Effects modest: 3.3% (age) and 5.3% (condition) of posterior in the ROPE.
limits: Bayes factors are only moderate. Older children's drift to multi-switch testing is a default shift with age, not proof of better CVS.
agent_relevance: The agent should choose its first test by its prior on how many causes there are, not by habit.

source: Bramley, Jones, Gureckis, Ruggeri (2022) Children's failure to control variables may reflect adaptive decision-making (strategy and accuracy)
finding: Over trials with 4 or more switches live (216 of 283 trials), older children used 'test one' less and 'test multiple' more, and the dense condition pushed toward test one. Only older children turned multi-switch tests into correct answers.
numbers: N=92 with full records (46 per age group). Test one: age OR 0.45 (BF 2.95), dense OR 2.41 (BF 4.33). Test multiple: age OR 2.93 (BF 7.2), dense OR 0.23 (BF 55.8). Correct guess among test-multiple users: older 17/19 (89%) vs younger 3/7 (43%), Fisher p=.003. Sparse: 15/15 vs 2/6, p=.002. Overall correct: sparse 62% (13/21) young, 88% (23/26) old; dense 64% (16/25) young, 50% (10/20) old.
limits: Small cells. Young children chose well but could not use the results. This separates test choice from inference.
agent_relevance: Choosing a good test and drawing the right conclusion from it are separate skills. A scaffold should check the inference step on its own, in code where possible (G2).

source: Peteranderl & Edelsbrunner (2020) Predictive value of children's understanding of indeterminacy and confounding for later mastery of the control-of-variables strategy
finding: Longitudinal study of 9-year-olds' understanding of indeterminacy of evidence and of confounding. Both predicted CVS skill two years later in planning, identifying and interpreting controlled experiments and in understanding why confounded comparisons are inconclusive. Holds with general cognition controlled.
numbers: N=170 second- to fourth-graders. The two precursors together explain 39% of later CVS mastery. Indeterminacy is the stronger overall predictor. Confounding better predicts the hard sub-skills (understanding inconclusiveness, planning a controlled experiment).
limits: Multiple-choice assessments, German school sample, observational. Gives prediction, not cause.
agent_relevance: Recognising 'this evidence cannot decide' is the root of one-change-per-test. An S4 gate could ask the agent to state what each test can and cannot rule out before running it.

source: Peteranderl & Edelsbrunner (2020) Predictive value of children's understanding of indeterminacy and confounding for later mastery of the control-of-variables strategy (review of earlier work, read in the paper)
finding: Background section: by about age 8 children prefer controlled over confounded comparisons (Bullock & Ziegler, LOGIC study), but spontaneous correct use is not found. Some adults never master CVS (Kuhn 2007).
numbers: Reported there for Bullock & Ziegler (1999): more than 50% of fourth graders, about 80% of fifth graders and almost all sixth graders justified choices by control of variables. Authors name ages 9-11 the critical period. All figures are as reported by Peteranderl & Edelsbrunner, not read in the original.
limits: Second-hand numbers. Recognition is easier than production.
agent_relevance: Recognising a good test is easier than producing one. Expect an LLM to verify a controlled design better than to write one unprompted.

source: Schwichow, Croker, Zimmerman, Hoffler, Hartig (2016) Teaching the control-of-variables strategy: a meta-analysis (as summarised by Peteranderl & Edelsbrunner 2020)
finding: CVS can be taught. Across 72 intervention studies the mean effect was moderate to large. Some studies show benefit for children as young as 6.
numbers: 72 intervention studies, mean overall g = 0.61.
limits: Seen only through the 2020 paper's summary. I did not open the 2016 paper (paywalled). Moderators not seen.
agent_relevance: Instruction in the rationale works for humans. For an agent, putting the rationale in the scaffold is the analogue.

source: Moeller, Sodian, Sobel (2022) Developmental trajectories in diagnostic reasoning: understanding data are confounded develops independently of choosing controlled tests
finding: Preschoolers (3-6) show some ability to recognise confounded evidence and to choose a controlled test, but the two abilities were unrelated. So choosing a controlled test may not rest on knowing that confounded data are inconclusive.
numbers: N=57 children aged 3-6. Controlled choice on 66% of two-variable trials and 43% of three-variable trials (task effect B=0.95, p<.001; no age effect). Said 'cannot know' on confounded-evidence trials 39% of the time; justified robustly on 22%. Age effect on knowledge claims B=0.09, p=.004.
limits: Chance levels differ between two- and three-option trials. Small N. A null correlation between abilities is weak evidence of independence.
agent_relevance: Procedural CVS and the explicit reason for it can come apart. An agent may follow 'one change' as a rule without knowing why. Guardrail G3 supplies the why in code.

source: Sobel, Koksal, Osterhaus, Bachhuber, Sodian (2026) Longitudinal relations between representational and advanced theory of mind and scientific reasoning, ages 4 to 7
finding: Theory of mind at age 4 predicts scientific reasoning at 5.5 and, through advanced theory of mind, at 7.5. Executive function and language also relate independently. Scientific reasoning here means integrating causal reasoning with the ability to represent and update the likelihood of hypotheses.
numbers: Three waves: 4, 5.5, 7.5 years. Relations hold with executive function and language controlled. Sample size not recorded here.
limits: Correlational. Measures are age-specific batteries.
agent_relevance: Theory-evidence coordination rests on representing one's own beliefs as beliefs. In an agent, that is an explicit hypothesis list kept apart from observations.

source: Schlatter, Molenaar, Lazonder (2020) Individual differences in children's development of scientific reasoning through inquiry-based instruction
finding: Fifth graders improved in scientific reasoning over a 5-week inquiry physics unit, but not equally on every component. Reading comprehension and maths skill explained part of the pretest-to-posttest gain.
numbers: N=138 fifth-graders, 5 weeks. Significant pretest-posttest gain on a written scientific reasoning test.
limits: Per-component effect sizes not recorded here. No control group named in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Skills are separable. Do not treat 'scientific reasoning' as one lump when designing S4 checks.

source: Freer, Lorch, Lorch, Calderhead (2011) Deconstructing the instruction of the control of variables strategy (SREE abstract; Studies 1-2)
finding: Teaching CVS works best when a teacher explains and the child also designs experiments. Interaction beats lecture. The pattern holds in high- and low-achieving schools, but low schools learn less.
numbers: Nearly 3000 fourth-graders from 96 classrooms across studies. Study 1 binary-choice test: instruction plus ramps design 72% > instruction only 65% > ramps only 57%. High vs low schools 82% vs 63% in the best condition. Study 2: with student interaction 80% vs 70% without.
limits: Conference abstract, not the full paper. Children who showed pretest mastery were excluded.
agent_relevance: Doing alone is the weakest route. A scaffold needs the rule plus a chance to apply it, not the rule alone or trials alone.

source: Freer et al. (2011) (Studies 3-4: examples and number of variables)
finding: Starting from confounded designs and fixing them beat showing only clean designs, especially in low-achieving schools. Teaching with 4 variables beat 2.
numbers: Study 3, immediate: high schools 84% (confounded examples) vs 73% (clean only); low schools 69% vs 56%, and the gap persisted at months and 2.5 years in low schools only. Study 4 (low schools): 4 variables 63% vs 2 variables 53% (chance); planning on paper had no effect.
limits: Abstract-level reporting, no test statistics given. Simplifying instruction hurt.
agent_relevance: Show the agent bad (confounded) tests and ask it to repair them. A 'repair the confounded plan' operator may teach more than clean templates.

source: Siler, Klahr, Willows, Magaro (2011) Effect of scaffolded causal identification on transfer of experimental design skills (SREE abstract)
finding: In a mostly low-SES sixth-grade sample, adding five questions that ask which variables could have caused an outcome helped far transfer and removed the dependence of the delayed score on the pretest. Near transfer was already high without them.
numbers: N=33 (19 computer tutor TED, 14 teacher lesson). Ramps posttest mastery (3 of 4 unconfounded) 88% added-questions vs 83% baseline. Delayed test: pretest-posttest correlation r(8)=+.22, p=.57 added-questions vs r(9)=+.67, p=.03 baseline and r(13)=+.79, p=.001 control. Benefit largest for lowest-knowledge students.
limits: Tiny N, quasi-experimental (classes not randomized between TED and control), abstract only.
agent_relevance: 'Which variables could have caused this?' is a causal-identification question an agent can answer in code before it accepts a test as clean.

source: Triona & Klahr (2007) Hands-on science: does it matter what students' hands are on? (summary of Triona & Klahr 2003 and Klahr, Triona, Williams 2007)
finding: Teaching children to design unconfounded comparisons works equally well with physical and virtual springs and transfers to physical ramps a week later. Many elementary children change several things at once without instruction.
numbers: Study 1: 92 fourth and fifth graders. Score about 20% at pretest, about 60% at posttest and transfer, no physical-virtual difference. Study 2: 56 seventh and eighth graders built mousetrap cars, physical vs virtual, discovery setting.
limits: Secondary summary of two papers. I did not open the originals.
agent_relevance: The medium of testing does not matter for learning the skill. A simulated environment is a fair proxy for a real one.

source: Morris, Croker, Zimmerman, Gill, Romig (2013) Gaming science: the gamification of scientific thinking
finding: Review. Scientific thinking does not routinely develop on its own. It needs cultural tools and teaching. Games can scaffold it through feedback and simulations.
numbers: No new data.
limits: A position paper. Quotes Kuhn & Franklin (2006).
agent_relevance: Supports adding explicit scaffolds rather than expecting the skill to appear.

source: Coenen, Ruggeri, Bramley, Gureckis (2019) Testing one or multiple: how beliefs about sparsity affect causal experimentation (as described in Bramley et al. 2022)
finding: Mathematical analysis: how efficient CVS is depends on causal sparsity. When few of many variables matter, testing about half of the remaining candidates per test (split-half) is far better. With one cause and equal priors, split-half is optimal.
numbers: Adult strategy gap between sparsity conditions 66 percentage points (as cited); the children study assumed a 40-point gap for its power analysis.
limits: Seen only through Bramley et al. I did not open the 2019 paper.
agent_relevance: Gives a formal rule: choose test size by expected information gain given beliefs about sparsity. This is the model to put in the S4 test chooser.

source: Klahr & Dunbar (1988) Dual space search during scientific reasoning
finding: Founding model of scientific discovery as search in two spaces, hypotheses and experiments, plus evidence evaluation. Adults programming a toy robot (BigTrak) split into theorists, who changed hypotheses often, and experimenters, who ran many tests. NOT OPENED: publisher returned 403.
numbers: Not recorded. Do not quote figures from this line.
limits: Source not read. Content is from general knowledge; Schlatter et al. 2020 cite it for 'hypothesizing, experimenting, evaluating evidence'.
agent_relevance: Matches the schema: states for hypothesis, test, evidence. The program should keep the two searches as separate counted steps.

source: Klahr, Fay, Dunbar (1993) Heuristics for scientific experimentation: a developmental study
finding: Children and adults on the BigTrak task. Children had more trouble than adults designing experiments that test hypotheses and generating alternative hypotheses. NOT OPENED: paywalled. Peteranderl & Edelsbrunner cite it for the view that elementary experimentation looks deficient.
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Source not read.
agent_relevance: Children stuck to one hypothesis and tested to confirm. Similar to the LLM confirmation bias in the Jhaveri 2026 line.

source: Chen & Klahr (1999) All other things being equal: acquisition and transfer of the control of variables strategy
finding: The canonical CVS study: direct instruction plus hands-on experience taught children in grades 2-4 to use and transfer CVS; unaided exploration did little. NOT OPENED: Wiley and OUP returned 403.
numbers: Not recorded. Do not quote figures from this line.
limits: Source not read. Triona & Klahr (2007) and Freer et al. (2011) describe it as the origin of the brief teaching intervention.
agent_relevance: Direct teaching of the rationale beat unaided discovery. Put the reason for one-change-per-test into the scaffold.

source: Klahr & Nigam (2004) The equivalence of learning paths in early science instruction: effects of direct instruction and discovery learning
finding: Third and fourth graders: many more learned CVS under direct instruction than under discovery, and those discovery learners who did learn transferred equally well. From memory only. NOT OPENED.
numbers: From memory, unverified: about 77% of direct-instruction children mastered CVS vs about 23% of discovery children.
limits: Not opened. Treat figures as a lead to check. Later work (Dean & Kuhn 2007, ERIC EJ760016, 'Direct instruction vs discovery: the long view') challenges the long-run claim.
agent_relevance: Fits the claim that the scaffold should state the rule. Check numbers before citing.

source: Kuhn, Garcia-Mila, Zohar, Andersen (1995) Strategies of knowledge acquisition
finding: Multi-week microgenetic study of multivariable causal systems. Participants often kept theory-driven, confirming strategies and changed several variables at once; improvement was slow. NOT OPENED.
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Source not read; that it shows children changing several things at once is stated in Triona & Klahr 2007 and Bramley et al. 2022.
agent_relevance: Kuhn's point is theory-evidence coordination: beliefs bend how evidence is read. G3 (check on data the answer was not fitted to) addresses this.

source: Tschirgi (1980) and Inhelder & Piaget (1958), as cited in Peteranderl & Edelsbrunner 2020
finding: Older work: the vary-one-thing rule was thought to appear only in adolescence, and whether a test is judged good depends on whether its outcome is wanted. NOT OPENED; only citation context read.
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Second-hand only.
agent_relevance: A test is judged by its outcome, not its design. The S4 gate should judge the plan before seeing results.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to falsify: evaluating and mitigating confirmation bias in language models
finding: Eleven LLMs played the Wason 2-4-6 rule-discovery game. They tend to propose triples that fit their current guess, so they find the rule more slowly. Telling models to consider counterexamples cut the bias and lifted success.
numbers: 11 LLMs, 45-turn limit, success from 6% to 78%. Mean success rose from 42% to 56% with the intervention prompt. Negative correlation between confirmation bias (incompatible:compatible test ratio) and success. Distilling the behaviour transferred to a Blicket task.
limits: Number-triple domain, simplified Wason task. Gains concentrated in thinking-mode models.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that an LLM's default is to confirm. A code-checked counterexample step is warranted when a hypothesis exists. Do not rely on a prompt alone.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Table 2 (Qwen3 and LLaMA results)
finding: Think-in-Opposites (TiO) prompting raised success for most models, but little for small non-thinking models. Dual-Goal prompting helped less and sometimes hurt.
numbers: Qwen3-32B thinking: baseline 0.41 to 0.60 with TiO; non-thinking 0.33 to 0.36. Qwen3-8B non-thinking 0.06 to 0.06. Qwen3-14B thinking 0.34 to 0.58. LLaMA-3.3-70B non-thinking 0.21 to 0.38. Qwen3-32B Dual-Goal non-thinking 0.10, below its 0.33 baseline.
limits: Read from a PDF table with garbled columns. Check alignment against the source before quoting.
agent_relevance: Prompting for falsification is model-dependent and can backfire. Measure per model; keep it behind a signal (G1).

source: Samiei et al. (2026) Human adults and LLMs as scientists: who benefits from active exploration? (CogSci 2026)
finding: Adults who choose their own interventions do well even on conjunctive causal rules, where passive adults do poorly. Proposing tests without seeing one's own outcomes was no better than passive watching. LLMs did not reliably gain from choosing interventions.
numbers: 306 adults (102 active, 102 passive yoked, 102 passive proposers). Conjunctive object identification: active 0.69, passive observer 0.45, passive proposer 0.12. Rule choice: 0.82, 0.69, 0.57. Humans averaged 9.6 tests (conjunctive) vs 6.4 (disjunctive).
limits: Four-object blicket-style task, text interface. The passive proposer group is a supplementary experiment.
agent_relevance: Planning a test is not enough. The loop from own test to own outcome is what teaches. Keep test and result reading in one closed loop.

source: Samiei et al. (2026) (LLM comparison)
finding: Six LLMs given the same action space (add, remove, test). Some match humans on final hypothesis accuracy but explore less efficiently. They show the same conjunctive-versus-disjunctive gap.
numbers: 6 models (gpt-5, gpt-5-mini, gemini-2.5-flash, deepseek-reasoner, o4-mini, deepseek-chat), 48 trials each, temperature 0. Mean tests conjunctive/disjunctive: gpt-5 10.2/7.7, gemini-2.5-flash 13.5/9.7, deepseek-reasoner 8.2/6.8, o4-mini 6.7/4.2, deepseek-chat 12.3/11.9; humans 9.6/6.4, top humans 8.5/3.8.
limits: Exact accuracy values were in a garbled figure and were not recorded. 24 trials per rule type is small.
agent_relevance: Test count and information gain per test can be computed in code, so the program can check whether the agent's tests actually narrow the hypothesis set.

source: Chen et al. (2026) ACED-Bench: evaluating how LLM agents acquire and act on causal evidence
finding: Benchmark where agents choose experiments on hidden causal models. Failures sit in the investigation: wrong intervention chosen, relevant evidence lost, or continuing after enough evidence. Final accuracy hides this.
numbers: ACED-CORE 180 tasks (60 ancestry/descendancy, 120 decision tasks). ACED-QUAL 150 yes/no questions, easier because the contrast is named. 7 contemporary and 2 older LLMs, 3 agent designs, four-turn budget. Several ACED-QUAL cells at or near ceiling.
limits: Per-model accuracy values not recorded here (in figures). Synthetic neuro-symbolic worlds.
agent_relevance: Strong LLMs use the sampling tool when told which contrast to test. The hard part is choosing the contrast. That is the S4 choice, so it needs a scaffold.

source: Gandhi, Li, Goodyear, Bhatia, Li, Bhaskar, Zaman, Goodman (2025) BoxingGym: benchmarking progress in automated experimental design and model discovery
finding: Ten generative-model environments scored by expected information gain (EIG) for experiment choice. Larger and closed models do better, but all current approaches struggle at experimental design and model discovery.
numbers: 10 environments; 32B beats 7B consistently; closed-source models generally beat open-source.
limits: Specific EIG numbers not recorded. A design benchmark, not a CVS test as such.
agent_relevance: EIG is a computable score for how informative a test is. The program can use it to pick or reject the agent's proposed test.

source: Absence check: DiscoveryWorld (Jansen et al. 2024) and ScienceWorld (Wang et al. 2022)
finding: I opened both papers and searched the text for 'control of variables', 'confound' and 'controlled experiment'. Neither frames its tasks as CVS tests. No CVS-specific numbers were found.
numbers: No matches in a text search of both PDFs (only unrelated uses of 'isolated' and 'ablate').
limits: Negative search result only; tasks may still need CVS implicitly. Not a full read.
agent_relevance: No ready benchmark of the exact S4 behaviour in these two. Our own S4 test needs a purpose-built task.
